extracted.intended_audience: general readers / internet-culture researchers documenting meme events
extracted.subtask_description: Create a wiki-style entry that documents the origin, spread, timeline, notable responses, and media coverage of a Twitter hashtag campaign or meme, with quotes and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of racial insensitivity as trigger for cancellation campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: #CancelColbert is a Twitter hashtag campaign launched to rally up support for the cancellation of Comedy Central's satirical news show The Colbert Report in March 2014 after the show host Stephen Colbert tweeted a joke that was perceived as racially insensitive towards Asian Americans on Twitter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents that perception alone—regardless of intent or context—can catalyze a large-scale hashtag campaign: the hashtag was tweeted over 49,000 times in less than 24 hours. Use this criterion to explain why a social-media backlash began.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and medium suitability for jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Salon’s piece questioned whether the joke, taken out of its context, was well-suited for the shortform microblogging service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a joke that caused controversy, note whether the joke was excerpted from a larger satirical segment and whether the platform (Twitter's shortform format) removed necessary context. The entry uses this principle to frame arguments that context and medium affect interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire targeting hypocrisy can still use language perceived as offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: In lampooning Snyder's contradictory stance on racial relations, Colbert proposed that he would start his own offensively named charity, saying: "I am willing to show Asian community I care by introducing the Ching-Chong Ding-Dong Foundation for Sensitivity to Orientals or Whatever."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document that satirical intent (criticizing hypocrisy) may employ racialized phrasing; the page implies that such phrasing can be read as punching down or as racially insensitive, and thus is central to why controversy arose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account attribution and who controls an account matters in public response
rubrics_metrics.description: The @ColbertReport account is an official Comedy Central account but not handled by Colbert or the show's writers; the entry quotes clarifying tweets: "For the record ColbertReport is not controlled by Stephen Colbert or his show."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion to explain how misunderstandings about who authored a post can affect who is held responsible and how audiences respond; clarifying authorship is a key mitigating step documented here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid clarification and response by creators can shape controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: The page records a sequence of responses: the @ColbertReport account clarifying it is not controlled by Colbert, a follow-up clarifying tweet with context, and Stephen Colbert tweeting from @StephenAtHome jokingly supporting #CancelColbert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting a meme controversy, include timestamps and text of official clarifications or responses; the entry uses these to show how quick public messaging (clarification, context link, creator response) factors into how the incident develops and is perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: News media coverage amplifies and frames social-media controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: The story was picked up by major news media outlets on March 28th, including TIME, The Huffington Post, and USA Today; several major websites published essays and think pieces about the larger context of the Twitter outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record which mainstream and opinion outlets covered or analyzed the event, since such coverage amplifies reach and frames the debate (examples given: TIME, HuffPost Live, Jezebel, Salon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice and counter-arguments from cultural commentators are part of the meme narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Jezebel published 'What We Can Learn From the Embarrassing #CancelColbert Shitstorm,' which outlined what fans should do when they believe their favorite show or celebrity is being unfairly attacked online; Salon defended the quip as a 'totally legitimate dig.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include references to prescriptive or defensive pieces (advice for fans, defenses of the joke) as they represent evaluative criteria and recommended actions within the discourse, even if the entry itself does not reproduce those recommendations in full.
